newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- FOMC, supply fill agenda.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- FOMC, supply fill agenda.

text.p: U.S. credit markets will start Wednesday on a quiet note as participants await the outcome of a Federal Reserve policy-setting meeting and the Treasury's announcement of its quarterly refunding effort.

"We have two big things tomorrow afternoon. The morning should be very, very quiet ... I suspect nothing is going to be happening in the early part of the session," said Jerry Zukowski, money market economist at PaineWebber Inc.
The Fed's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will conclude its two-day meeting on Wednesday. The outcome is expected to be announced at around 1415 EST/1915 GMT.
As far as forecasts go, an overwhelming majority of Wall Street analysts believe the Fed will keep monetary policy on hold and short-term interest rates unchanged.

"We don't expect anything out of the Fed tomorrow," said Michelle Colley Laughlin, Treasury market strategist at Prudential Securities Inc. PaineWebber's Zukowski agreed. So did Jonathan Bassile, an economist with HSBC Markets Inc.
"We see no change in policy. They won't move because inflationary pressures haven't really emerged and a lot of different indicators ... remain pretty benign," Bassile said.

Recent data, including fourth quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and the January industry report from the National Association of Purchasing Management, suggested the economy remains in a steady growth pace with no sign of inflation.
Analysts said U.S. credit markets were expected to remain calm and rangebound if the FOMC's decision turns out to be in line with expectations.

"The Treasury market is expected to stay mostly where it is if the Fed doesn't do anything," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank. "If nothing happens, people will immediately begin to focus on the payroll report."
The January non-farm payroll report will be released on Friday, February 7.

Traders said, however, the benchmark 30-year bond yield could easily jump to 6.90 percent from its current level of 6.71 percent if the Fed surprised the market with a 25-basis-point hike in the federal funds rate on Wednesday.
Fed funds are currently targeted at 5.25 percent.
The market will also pay close attention to the announcement of the Treasury's quarterly refunding auctions.
In a Reuters poll, analysts expect the refunding effort to total $37.5 bilion, made up of $17.5 billion of three-year notes, $10.0 billion of 10-year notes and $10.0 bilion in 30-year bonds.
On the economic data front, the market will take in December factory orders. The headline number is expected to be down 0.8 percent against a 0.4 percent decline in the previous month.
The 6-1/2-percent benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was quoted up 12/32 at 97-10/32 in late trading on Tuesday. Its yield was at 6.71 percent.
The Fed added reserves to the banking system on Tuesday through 14-day fixed system repurchase agreements when federal funds were trading at 5-3/16 percent. The operation totalled $4.113 billion.
Fed funds are seen opening at 5.19 percent on Wednesday.
